a.notes: The track series is far ahead for the owner. It is the line language the owner called "high style" (stops, rings, buffers, timetable margins), it now runs through Home, To do, Chat, Plans, setup and Status, and its ink plates put grounded, material colour into the content, not into a corner wash. Trued, Relit is the best: the starters branching off the greeting box on a steel line is the kind of line art the owner wants echoed, and the tube as stop one with tube-height plates gives Coming up real presence. Grafts that worked: Ticked's one-line setup strip and its tick-on-the-line for To do; Chat's left track with times in the margin; Printed's lit wire feeding the board and its sunk date windows; Diary in Ink's ink tags; Pocket Diary, Lit's lit voice for the machine (strong DNA return). Grafts that did not: Diary in Ink's amber italic-mono 'pencil' looks like a costume, and Hung's three-column Home crowds the box. Instrumented's spend meter is worth taking into whichever track design wins, but as a mutant it changes too little elsewhere. The timetable line has the best grounded solids (enamel keys), but its lines are too faint away from Home; the pocket line has the best glass (the mini-month), but a dim spine. Glow check: Relit and Trued put the halo back on the greeting, the tube and the lamps without glare; Ticked runs slightly hot at the top.

scores.why: The original glow DNA, but it is the Matrix wash the owner asked to calm: about 83% green, no grounded companion, and the boxes are generic. It is still titled 'What's on your mind?'.

Calm and well built, with good grounded slate. But its line art is thin, the phosphor lives mostly in the glass, and it keeps the old title. It is a fair yardstick, and this heat's track designs pass it.

Lit Sill Line still has real soul: the now lamp and lit run feed the tube, the To do lamps sit in a timetable margin, the Ideas 'line from home' scope glows, and the ink plates are grounded. Its loose placement (the Coming up label stranded under the rail, the 'All plans' link floating) is now beaten by its own children.

Trued's system is clean and the setup track is lovely. Home's greeting is the weakest of the series, though: a plain box with starters floating to its right, and an empty Coming up stub before the tube.

The rail now leaves the now lamp and runs under the tube to the plates, all in reading order. Status's lamp board with its named rows reads as an instrument. The Ideas scope keeps the line language on a list page. The long lit run and the empty glass above Coming up are the faults, and the board's lower left glares a little.

This is the closest yet to what the owner praised in Signal Box. The greeting's steel branch of starters with ring stops is high-style line art. The tube is stop one on the rail, and the ink plates the tube's height carry grounded blue-black and a cyan cap in the page content. The Status strip joins glass and lamps, and the glow is back on the greeting and its tube. It loses a little on the plain Ideas table (the scope is gone) and on the month's per-week rails, which run heavy.

The grafts do work. The one-line setup strip frees Home, the To do ring is the tick you press, Chat hangs from a left track with times in the margin and a lit 'your turn' ring, and the dashed quiet week on Plans is a nice touch. Home is still green-led (about 69%), and the big lit 'planning' with the tube's halo makes the top heavy with light.

The moving-coil spend meter on Status is a real instrument and suits the CRT, and the six-signal lamp family is tidy. Outside Status it is its parent, nearly pixel for pixel. That is the 'nearly identical' the owner warned about.
Vera's line from the box is a good idea, but the page is about 89% green and the grounded colour lives only in hairlines. The departure board is lovely, though.

The enamel interchange keys (denim, teal and plum plates labelled 'usually Plans' and so on) are exactly the grounded, solid colour with a job the owner asked for, and they sit in the page content. The board beside the box is calm. The plum leans off-period, and To do, Status and Settings get only thin rails, so the line language is faint away from Home.

Home reads best of the timetable line. Her line runs from the box through the starters to a departure board fed at its head by a lit wire. On To do, the sunk readout windows with amber rings for late are a smart timetable margin. The kids' wishes sit off the rail, Plans and Status are generic, and 'Tell Vera our plans.' with its full stop is awkward.

The hung margin and the condensed sign face are good typesetting ideas. But the three-column Home crowds the box, the chat loses its one non-green line, and at a glance it reads as the parent with narrower type.
The Now/Next/Later spine and the glass mini-month on Plans have real CRT charm. Status and Ideas, though, are plain lists hanging from a dim line, and the grounded colour is sparse.

A tidier diary. The kind index on Ideas, the key on Status and the unboxed groups all help, and the glass month is still the best calendar glass in the heat. The spine is too faint to lead the eye the way the track lines do, and the setup list still takes a whole column.

The blue-black ink who-tags and wells are a grounded material colour placed in the content. The one-line setup stop frees the shelf so To do stands by the box. The amber monospace-italic 'pencil' for 'was due…' looks like a costume rather than handwriting, and four voices plus VT323 is a lot of faces.

It brings back exactly the DNA the owner asked for: Vera's lines as small lit screens, the prompt glowing, and Send lit from within, while the family's words stay matte. It is a clear and convincing rule. It nudges the green back up, and the '6 worth a look' amber alarm on Status still shouts.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the greeting board with its steel branch of starters, the tube hung as stop one with tube-height ink plates (blue-black with a cyan cap and sunk time wells), the joined Status strip (glass, lamp board and tally), and the setup track. Fixes: (1) bring back the Ideas 'line from home' scope from Sill Line over the table, because Ideas is now the one page without line art or phosphor; (2) on the month, draw the week rails only on weeks that hold a plan and fade the empty ones to a hairline, because five full rails through the grid read heavy; (3) balance the plate names by words, not length, so proper names do not break ('Mount St. / Helens'); (4) on the phone, give the chevron in 'who is asking?' its room and shorten the Google note to one line; (5) move the worked-out values into views.py. Title: keep 'What's the plan?' or switch to 'What's our plan?'.

Keep the one-line setup strip with its three rings, To do's ring-you-press on the line, Chat's left track with its time margin and lit 'your turn' ring, the dashed quiet weeks on Plans, and the Status lamp board. Fixes: halve the halo on the large 'planning' and the tube's airglow, so the light sits on the key word and the tube, not across the top third. Shorten the title to 'What's our plan?' so the lit word is short. Show the ways-to-start keys on a phone as a stacked steel branch (as Trued, Relit does), not a sideways scroll. Give Lately added the same ink plate material as Coming up, so Home's lower half carries some grounded colour.

Keep the rail that runs from the now lamp under the tube to the plates, the Status lamp board with its tally beside it, and the Ideas scope. Fixes: shorten the lit run so it stops at the tube's stop and the later stretch is steel. Close the roughly 100px of empty glass above Coming up by hanging the starters under the box. Make the plates the tube's height, as Relit does, so the plans read as solid grounded things and not thin labels.

Keep the board fed at its head by a lit wire from Vera's line, and the sunk readout windows with amber rings on To do. Fixes: put the kids' wishes on the line as a stop, or move them to the right column. Carry the enamel interchange keys from Platformed (denim, teal, steel; drop the plum) onto the ways to start, so Home has solid grounded colour. Give Status and Plans a line of their own (lamps as stops, week rails). Retitle to 'What's our plan?', which drops the glowing full stop.

Keep the rule that the machine's words glow and the family's stay matte, with Vera's lines as small lit screens and the primary key lit from within. Graft in Diary in Ink's blue-black who-tags and the one-line setup stop, so the green has a grounded partner. Make the Now/Next/Later spine steel and slightly heavier so it leads the eye, and give it lamps at its stops. Turn the Status '6 worth a look' to plain words with one amber half-lamp.

Keep the enamel interchange keys with their 'usually Plans' and 'usually To do' notes: grounded colour with a job, in the content. Swap the plum for a period-correct steel-cyan or a muted CGA blue. Draw To do and the Status lamps as ring stops on a visible steel line, so the line language holds beyond Home.

a.titles: "What's our plan?" (t3-track-refine, t3-timetable-refine, t3-timetable-mut, t3-pocket-refine) and "What's the plan?" (t3-track-refine2) say the job best: they are short, in the family's voice, ask to be told something, fit one line on a phone, and light the job word with a short glow. Of the two I prefer "What's our plan?" for its 'our'. "What needs planning?" (t3-track-graft) is a good invitation and cannot be answered no, but the long lit word makes the glow heavy. "What should we plan?" (t3-pocket-graft) is fine but softer. "What are we planning?" (t2-track-graft, t3-track-mut) reads as a status check. "Anything to plan?" (t3-pocket-mut, t2-pocket-graft) is casual and can be answered 'no'. "Tell Vera our plans." (t3-timetable-graft) names her but is an order, not an invitation, and the full stop beside the glow is awkward.

a.notes: Through the phosphor lens, the strongest move in this heat is light that does a job: the tube's power wire feeding a lit run (track), a lit wire feeding a dot-matrix board (timetable), and light that marks who is speaking (pocket-mut). Grafts that worked: the rail name in the line's break and the one-strip setup (track-graft), the wire feeding NEXT UP and the leader-dot board rows (timetable-graft), and the setup collapsing to one amber spine node (pocket-graft). Grafts that worked less well: the graphite italic pencil and the blue who-tags (pocket-graft), which drift off the tube's world, and the amber date pills on timetable-graft's To do, which compete with the light. Shrinking the tube (t2-track-refine, t3-track-refine2) costs the most soul: the monitor should stay the page's one real green screen. t3-timetable-mut adds fine typesetting but takes the light down and leaves Chat monochrome. Dice graphics on Status (t3-track-mut's meter) are a phosphor win worth spreading across lineages.

scores.why: All the original light is here (bloom on the tube, glowing dots, halo on 'mind'), but it is lit everywhere at once. The Matrix wash spends the glow on every surface, so none of it means anything.

A real green screen at the desk, with grounded colour around it and the glow kept for the terminal and its readouts. It is calm and alive, though the light is spread thinly over a lot of small mono text.
The tube's power wire drops into a breathing NOW lamp, and the lit run glows across the sill with airglow under it. It reads as a signal box at night, with the light only on what is live.
The tube is shrunk into a card among the plates and the lit run is short. The light is correct but timid: the board is mostly steel and the phosphor soul is thin.

The full-width haloed box with 'plan' in two layers is a strong lit greeting, and the long lit run into the tube's stop glows well. But the tube is now smaller than the box, the run's glare pools at the lower left, and the box's halo competes with the tube for first light.

The greeting is its own lit board (pool, raster, a box that turns green while typing, a hot core on 'plan'), and the tube powers on beautifully. But the tube is shrunk to a plate's height, so the monitor is no longer a hero, and the lit run is only one stop long.

This heat's best balance of light. The big 'planning' headline glows over the box, the tube's power wire feeds the lit run with airglow, the 'Coming up' plate sits in a break of the lit line, and below the sill everything is matte slate and steel. One luminous zone, then calm.

Home is the parent's light. Status gains a real phosphor instrument: scanlined glass, a moving-coil meter glowing in green, haloed lamps where something works and dark sockets where it does not. That is the green screen's soul in its most fitting place, though the needle sits idle at zero.
The dot-matrix board and the lit spine are good phosphor ideas. But the page is about 89% green, so the glow is everywhere and the board is small beside a busy three-column layout.

The departures board is a true dot-matrix tube with leader dots, and Vera's spine is lit to her terminus. But the enamel keys and the board compete beside the box, and the light feels distributed rather than led.

The lit wire leaves the spine at NEXT UP and feeds a big departure board: a radar, mono rows with leader dots and a scanline footer. It is the most convincing 1980s screen in the heat, and the phosphor stops where the board ends. The amber date pills on To do are a little loud.
The type pairing is handsome and the hung margin is a typographer's pleasure, but it adds no light. Chat goes back to near-monochrome green (97%), and the three columns dilute the board.
NOW and NEXT are lit tabs on a glowing spine, and the tube carries a radar plus a waveform of the coming weeks: genuine instrument light. The rest is quiet slate.
Light sits only on NOW, the box's lit floor and the tube, with grounded rows below. It is honest and calm, but it changes little from its parent in phosphor terms.

The ink and pencil hands are an original idea, but the Victor Mono italic 'pencil' and the many blue tags pull away from the tube's world, and the amber scrawls compete with the light. The phosphor survives only in the top half.

It is the only design that gives the glow a rule: what the machine says is lit (Vera's chat screens with a rim and bloom, her times, the cursor prompt, a lit NOW plate) and what the family writes stays matte. That is the CRT's soul as meaning, not decoration. The dim-lit placeholder risks reading as typed text.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the glowing headline over the box, the tube's power wire into the lit run, and the 'Coming up' plate in the line's break; give the run its sweep-on again (only its head moves now). Fixes: drop the headline's halo by one layer, because at this size 'planning' outshines the tube. Graft t3-track-mut's Status instrument (the meter beside the lamp board) in place of today's glass. Let the To do 'now' rule carry a faint afterglow so the lower page has one live light. Give Chat's lit ring at the box E4's halo.

Keep the moving-coil meter and the named lamp board, and bring back E20 breathing on the working lamps, at least on Status. Show the needle off zero (a usual-day bug that is visible, an amber zone that is drawn). Carry the six-signal family to Home with a key, and make the halftone band visible or drop it.

Keep the lit wire feeding NEXT UP and the dot-matrix board with leader dots and the radar. That is this heat's best tube. Turn To do's amber date pills into sunk dark windows with only an amber ring, so the warm colour does not fight the board. Thin the spine's glow below the box to a hairline, keeping the lit stops, so the line reads lit only from now to next. Light the chat's newest timestamp window in phosphor.

Keep the rule 'the machine speaks in light, the family writes matte', and Vera's chat screens with their rim and bloom. Let the prompt glow only once the box has focus, so it is not mistaken for typed text. Soften the older Vera bubbles to rim-only and keep the bloom for the newest. Drop the footer key and replace the '6 worth a look' amber alarm with a half lamp.

Make the board the one lit object in the right column (put Lately added under it in matte), and let the ways-to-start enamel keys go matte slate with only the stub coloured, so the box and board own the light.

Give the tube its height back (the monitor must be the hero, not a plate), and let the lit run go at least to the second stop. Keep the greeting board's raster pool and the box turning green while someone types.

Set the pencil in an upright quiet face, not a script italic, and cut the who-tags to bone text without the blue fills. Keep the setup stop collapsing to one amber node on the spine: that grafted feature worked.

a.titles: The best is 'What's our plan?' (t3-track-refine, the timetable refine and mutant, t3-pocket-refine): the family's own voice, the job in one word, a short lit word that glows cleanly. 'Tell Vera our plans.' (t3-timetable-graft) is a strong second. It names who hears you and is an imperative invitation, which suits a timetable whose line is Vera's, though the full stop is a little stiff. 'What needs planning?' works and the lit word ends the line, but 'planning' is a heavy glow at headline size. 'What should we plan?' is fine but soft. 'What's the plan?' reads as a status check, less as an invitation. 'Anything to plan?' fails because it can be answered 'no'. 'What are we planning?' reads as a status question.

a.notes: Through this lens the track series leads the heat: it is the one lineage whose Home looks like nothing else, while its grounded steel, slate and ink plates keep the green to the lit run and the tube. What worked among the grafts: in Ticked, the question promoted to the board's headline, the rail's name set in a break of the run, and setup shrunk to a three-ring strip. In Printed, the lit wire feeding the departure board at its head. In Diary in Ink, the ink who-tags. Platformed's enamel interchange keys are the best grounded colour in the heat and should travel. What did not work: Diary in Ink's stacked pencil italics read as costume, and Hung's condensed face plus hung quotes is a type swap that cramps the box without reshaping the page. On the owner's 'bring back the phosphor': the most persuasive answers give the light a meaning. Those are Pocket Diary, Lit's lit machine voice in Chat, Relit's pooled greeting board and Printed's lit rail, rather than more glow everywhere. The single best object in the heat is Instrumented's Status faceplate with its moving-coil spend meter. Whichever track design wins should adopt it, because a family would say 'oh, that's lovely' at it.

scores.why: It has the original tube's charm, with real bloom and a lit word, but every surface is the same green-on-black card, so it reads as Matrix costume rather than an identity.
A calm, competent desk terminal with good grounding. It is the safe reference: tasteful, but no single image a family would remember.
The lit run from the now lamp to the tube's wire, with the plates hanging off the rail, is a real signature. The box beside the tube splits the eye, and the setup board is a second, weaker diagram.
The tube hung as stop one of the rail is a clever idea, but the board is busy: the starters float right of the box and the lit run is short, so the light never takes the page.

The full-width box is handsome and the long lit run glows well. The tube now floats under the box with no rail of its own, there is a big dead patch of glass, and the plates have shrunk to labels, so the board reads less like one diagram than its parent.

The most material board in the heat. The tube is the first plate on the line, ink plates carry kind rings, a sunk time well and who it is for, and a steel branch of starters leaves the box like a siding. The greeting board's pool and raster bring the phosphor back exactly where it belongs. It feels like a real signal box at night.

The boldest composition: the question as the board's headline, the tube's wire dropping onto the lit Coming up rail, the rail's name set in a break of the line, and setup shrunk to a tiny three-ring track in an amber-edged strip. To do's dated margin with rings you press makes the line do work. It is memorable, coherent across pages, and lit only where it is live.

Status's instrument panel (a named lamp board beside a moving-coil spend meter with a lit needle and $0.00 in VT323) is the single most delightful object in the heat. Elsewhere it is its parent untouched, so the page as a whole moves little.
The station line down the box, with the dot-matrix board beside it, is a clear idea. The three columns feel like a dashboard and the line is thin, so the timetable mood is only hinted at.

The enamel interchange keys (denim, teal and plum faces with 'usually Plans / To do / Ideas') are the heat's best grounded colour with a job, and the terminus ring is lovely. The board and the right column are plain, so the station mood stops at the left column.

The lit rail running down the left, feeding the departure board at its head, is the strongest use of phosphor as wayfinding in this lineage. The amber date windows on To do are crisp. The right column of banded rows is generic, and 'Tell Vera our plans.' gives the page a confident voice.

Barlow Condensed signs and hung quote marks give real typographic personality, a station sign-painter's hand. The three narrow columns cramp the box, Chat goes almost wholly green, and the hang is barely visible, so the style reads as a font swap more than a system.
NOW, NEXT and LATER tabs on one spine is a clear, original structure, and the tube with its four-week trace is charming. The tracked label tabs feel a little costume, and the right column floats.
A tidy diary: square nodes, unboxed groups, and Vera's tab sitting on the box like a page divider. It is calm and coherent, but the tidying has taken some of the personality out with it.

Two hands is a genuinely new idea: graphite pencil italic for how far off things are, blue-black ink tags for who they are for. It feels like a diary someone keeps. The pencil face edges toward costume and there are five faces in all, but the material story is the most original in the lineage.

One clear rule, 'what the machine says gives off light', turns Vera's chat lines into small lit screens beside the family's matte slips. This is the most persuasive answer in the heat to 'bring back the phosphor', because the light now carries a meaning. Home and Settings change little.

fixes.suggestion: Keep: the question as the board's headline, the tube's wire dropping onto the lit rail, 'Coming up · 4 coming' set in a break of the run, the three-ring setup strip, and To do's dated margin with press-rings. Fix Home: the plates are small and identical. Take refine2's plate anatomy (kind ring, a sunk time well, who it is for) so the plans carry grounded colour and are worth looking at. The starter keys sit loose between the box and the rail; hang them as a short steel siding off the box, as refine2 does. Lately added's right-aligned kind words read as a column of grey; drop them, or set them in small caps beside the name. Graft track-mut's Status instrument panel in place of the current glass.

Keep: the tube as stop one's plate, the ink plates with sunk time wells, the steel starter branch with its 'Or start with' head, and the lit greeting board with its pool and raster. Fix: the greeting box is wide but short, and 'What's the plan?' at its size leaves the board's lower half empty, so give the title more scale (about 3rem) or let the box run to the board's right edge on desktop. Coming up's four columns break 'Mount St. Helens' badly; balance by words, not length. The setup board's three rings on a long steel line are bland; take track-graft's compact strip. Bring the Status meter from track-mut.

Keep the Status faceplate exactly as it is: the named lamp board and the moving-coil spend meter are a standard-setting graphic. Fix: show the meter's scale on a log or usual-day basis so $0.04 is not pinned at zero, and carry the six-signal family onto Settings and To do with a one-line key. It belongs in whichever track design wins, not as a design of its own.

Keep: the lit rail down the left that feeds the departure board at its head, the board's printed rows with dot leaders, and the amber date windows on To do. Fix: the right column (Finish setting up, To do, Lately added) is a stack of generic banded cards with no station language. Give To do the same rail and stop rings, so the timetable continues across the page. Bring in Platformed's enamel interchange keys for the ways to start. They are the lineage's best grounded colour. The kids' wishes, sitting off the rail on the left, should either join it as a stop or move right.

Keep the enamel keys with their 'usually Plans' notes and the terminus ring. Fix: Home's right column is plain, so make Coming up's board taller and the column's heads match the left's station type. Lately added's dotted leaders to grey kind words look like a table of contents; tie each to its kind's enamel colour.

Keep the rule that the machine's voice is lit: Vera's chat screens with rims and halos, the lit NOW tab on the box, and the prompt cursor. Fix: on Home, Vera's tab and the tube are the only machine voices, so light Coming up's relative times ('in 7 days') as dim readouts and leave the family's titles matte. Take Diary in Ink's ink who-tags for the family's side, so both hands appear on one page. Replace 'Anything to plan?' with 'What's our plan?'. The amber '6 worth a look' on Status should become a quiet count.

Keep: the ink who-tags, the setup collapsed to one amber stop on the spine, and To do beside the box. Fix: the Victor Mono pencil italic ('in 7 days') is charming once but stacked amber pencil notes on To do look like a font demo. Keep pencil for Coming up's distances only, and set late words in the voice face in amber. Cut to three faces. Graft Pocket Diary, Lit's lit Vera screens in Chat.

a.titles: The best are 'What's our plan?' (Kept, Platformed, Hung and Trued) and 'What needs planning?' (Ticked). 'What's our plan?' is the family's own kitchen-table question: warm, short, in the 'us' voice, and its lit word is the app's job. 'What needs planning?' is the strongest invitation of the set, because it cannot be answered 'no' and it pulls in reminders and wishes as well as weekends. Its lit word ends the line and sits well as a board headline. 'What's the plan?' (Relit) is close behind, breezier and more colloquial, but a little less the family's own. 'Tell Vera our plans.' (Printed) has character and names who listens, which suits a timetable, but as an imperative with a full stop it reads more as an instruction than an invitation. 'What should we plan?' (Diary in Ink) is fine but flat. The ones that fail: 'Anything to plan?' (Lit), which invites 'no, thanks', and 'What are we planning?' (Instrumented), which reads as a status check on plans already made and lights a heavy 8-letter word.

a.notes:
The heat's two strongest systems arrive at the brief from opposite directions. Trued, Relit makes the rail and the plate the structure, and its grounded solids (ink plates, sunk wells, slate keys) each have one job. Platformed puts its grounded colour in the enamel keys, which carry information ('usually Plans'). Both bring the light back only to the box, the tube and the lamps, which is what the owner asked for.

Grafts that worked:
- track-graft's one-line setup strip (better than any boxed setup notice in the heat).
- the kind labels moved to the left of their rings.
- timetable-graft's wire feeding the board at its head.
- pocket-graft's ink who-tags.

Grafts that did not work:
- timetable-graft's amber date pills, which read as warnings.
- the fully lit rails (timetable-graft, track-refine), which bring back glare.
- pocket-graft's mono-italic pencil, which costs readability and adds a fifth face.

Dice mutants:
- track-mut's instrument panel is the best single element here and should be grafted into the track and timetable Status pages.
- timetable-mut's hung punctuation is genuine typesetting, but it lost the enamel.

Across the lineages, line-heaviness is the shared risk. Rails earn their place where there is an order (Coming up, To do, setup, chat) and cost clarity on the month grid.

scores.why: A coherent kit, but monochrome glare: every card has the same green-edged box, nothing has its own job, and Home is a stack of equal tiles with no reading order.

A disciplined desk: ink and slate do the work and the terminal glows where it should. Home is a dense set of panels, though, and its tracked mono labels and boxed sections give it less hierarchy than the best of this heat.
Has the soul (the now lamp, the lit run, the tube's wire), but the parts are out of reading order: the question sits beside the tube and the sill zone is half empty.
Branch lines are a clean system on To do and the setup steps, but Home's box floats over a separate Coming up board and the light is thin.

The order is right: full-width box, then one rail from the now lamp through the tube to the plates, with an amber-edged setup board below. But the box is wide and empty, about 100px of dead glass sits under the starters, and the 24rem lit run is the brightest thing below the fold.

The most complete system in the heat. The question board has its starters on a steel branch, and Coming up is one rail with the tube as stop one and plates of the same height, each with a sunk time well. Setup is one stepped line, the wells and plates recur on the month, and Status opens on a glass strip of lamps over a tally. The weak spots are the month's per-week rails, which are heavy, and Home To do's crowded left margin of times.

Two grafts earn their place: setup folded into one compact amber strip ('Next: choose your own password'), and kind labels set left of their rings in Lately added. But the headline floats top right, cut off from Vera's name and the tube, and the long lit rail through the board's lower edge is glare.
Status's instrument panel is the best single element in the heat: a named lamp board, a moving-coil spend meter and one family of six signals. Every other page is pixel-identical to its parent.
A tidy three-column station, but 89% green, with the departures board out-glowing the box.

The brief's 'grounded colour in solid things with a job', done literally. The enamel interchange keys (denim, teal, plum) each name where the answer usually goes, and Vera's line runs from her screen through the box to a lit terminus. The dot-leader departure board prints row by row as it powers on, and the same rail with ring stops carries on through To do, Status and Settings. Status is the flattest page, and the board's VT323 rows are small.

The board fed by a lit wire is a nice idea. But the rail is lit green along its whole length (glare), and the amber-edged date pills on To do read as warning badges on every row; it is 83% green again.

The hung margin is real typesetting: markers outside one text edge, and a condensed sign face paired with a humanist voice. But the quote marks on the starters suggest the quotes are sent, the enamel is gone (Chat is 97% green), and the three columns squeeze the box.
A clear Now/Next/Later spine with diary dates, but boxed groups on Settings and Status, and the amber is used for things that are not late.

The spine is a rule that holds on every page (Home, Plans' weeks, To do, Status, Ideas), with diary-set dates, unboxed hairline groups and Status's headline tally. The right column empties below To do, Settings' index is still tiles, and the outlined amber checkboxes on late tasks lean toward warning.
The blue-black ink who-tags are good grounded solids with a job. The graphite-italic mono pencil ('was due 5 days ago') is hard to read, and four text faces plus VT323 is too wide a type system.
Lighting the machine's voice is a principled rule, but the glowing prompt reads as words already typed, and the lit times add green without adding hierarchy.

a.titles: The best is "What's our plan?" (t3-track-refine, t3-timetable-refine, t3-timetable-mut, t3-pocket-refine). It says the job in one word, 'our' makes it the family's own question, it fits one line on a phone, and 'plan' is a short lit word that sits well at display size. "What's the plan?" (t3-track-refine2) comes a close second: more colloquial, but without the ownership. "What needs planning?" (t3-track-graft) is a fair invitation, but the 8-letter lit word is heavy at that size and the -ing form drags. "Tell Vera our plans." (t3-timetable-graft) names who listens, but as an imperative statement it reads less as the box's question, and the period needs its own span to dodge the glow. Three fail: "Anything to plan?" invites 'no'; "What should we plan?" reads as asking Vera for suggestions rather than telling her; "What are we planning?" reads as a status check.

a.notes:
Every design except timetable-graft (one target under 44px) clears the 44px target floor, and every Home Tab order goes box, then select, then Send, then starters. So the differences through this lens are in sight lines and in what the eye meets first.

The two designs that put the question first and widest and then answered it in one band beneath (track-refine2, timetable-refine) read best. Those that let the tube or To do sit beside or before the question (track-graft, track-refine, timetable-mut, the t2 timetable) lose the title-first order.

Grafts that worked:
- track-graft's one-line setup strip with 'Next: ...', and pocket-graft's equivalent line: both much faster to scan than a setup card.
- timetable-graft's board fed from the rail.
- track-refine2's tube as stop one in a row of equal plates.
- timetable-refine's 'usually Plans/To do/Ideas' hints on the starters, the single best comprehension addition in the heat.

Grafts that did not work:
- pocket-graft's bordered who-tags and timetable-graft's outlined date windows: both make readouts look like buttons.
- Ring-as-checkbox on track-graft's To do: elegant, but the affordance is weak.
- pocket-mut's lit placeholder: it can be mistaken for typed text.
- track-mut's tiny six-signal family: hard to tell apart.

All three lineages beat today's page on the owner's 'reflect the page content' test. The track and timetable leaders now match or pass the Desk Terminal yardstick on how quickly a family member finds the next plan and the one thing to press.

scores.why: Yardstick. The question is clear, but Home is a stack of boxed cards with equal weight, To do shows ISO dates, and 42 of its 55 targets are under 44px. Squinted, the hierarchy flattens into green slabs.

Yardstick. Every target is 44px or more and it has a clear desk layout, but the question sits inside the monitor's glass and the tube leads the Tab order (Oaks Park and '3 plans' come before the box), so the eye and the keyboard both meet Next up before the one action.

Carried. The tube is first on the left and the title sits to its right, so the sight line lands on the monitor before the question. The lit run is legible, but Coming up's label and plates are spread across the board's lower half.

Carried. The question comes first and is clear, and the starters sit in a column beside it. The tube as stop one on Coming up's rail reads well, but the plates are small and the starters' column floats without a link to the box.

The full-width question box is read first, which is good. Below it the tube sits low on the left, the starters float in the middle and 'Coming up' is set mid-board over small plates, with about 100px of dead glass: the eye zig-zags after the box.

The clearest reading order in the heat: question, then a steel branch of starters (each a full-width key with an arrow saying it goes somewhere), then one Coming up row. On that row the tube is stop one and each plan is an equal plate with its kind, who it is for and its time in a sunk well. Setup is three numbered rings, and To do carries full date and time in the margin. On the phone the starters stack at full width. Squinted, it still reads as three bands.

The large headline question is read first, and the setup strip (1-2-3 rings plus 'Next: choose your own password →') is the best one-glance setup in the heat. But the tube still sits beside the title and competes with it. On To do the ring-as-tick has no checkbox look, so a press is not obvious and an amber ring reads 'late' rather than 'press'. On the phone the starters scroll sideways, hidden.

Status's lamp board puts every lamp's name beside it, and the spend meter is a quick glance answer. But the six signals are 14px and close in shape, the key is only on Status, and the meter crowds zero. Outside Status nothing changes for the user.
Carried. The three columns put To do first on the left, so the eye starts on a list rather than the question, and the box is squeezed into a narrow middle column.

The box is first, largest and widest. Each starter carries 'usually Plans / To do / Ideas', which tells a newcomer where things go: the best comprehension aid in the heat. 'Continue with Vera' is a clear terminus. The departure board lists every plan at a glance, setup is one compact amber notice, and To do's Now line splits late from upcoming. Squinted, the two columns and the lit box hold.

It has a strong order: question, starters, a board fed from the rail, Continue. The slim setup bar at the top right ('Choose your own password › 2 more') is efficient. But To do's amber-outlined date windows look like buttons, the wishes hang off the rail out of Tab sense, and one Home target is under 44px.

To do in the left column is read before the question. The quoted starters suggest the quotes are sent, and the box is narrow and wraps its placeholder. The condensed sign face is quick to scan but light at label sizes.
Carried. The Now/Next/Later spine explains the order at a glance, but 'Anything to plan?' invites a 'no', setup takes the whole right column, and the tube pushes Coming up below the fold.

Now, Next and Later tags make the time order readable without instructions. Coming up rows are the most legible dates in the heat (large day, month, time, title, how far). Setup is a numbered list and To do sits beside the box. The tube still costs a screen of height before Coming up, and the setup list's long link text runs to two lines each.

The one-line setup ('3 steps · Next: Choose your own password · See all 3') and To do beside the box are both good for finding things. But the ink who-tags are bordered chips that look like buttons, the pencil Victor Mono italic is slow to read, and four faces is a lot to learn.
The glowing prompt in the box can be read as text already typed. Lighting the family's own plan times blurs the rule that 'lit means live or press here', and the amber '6 worth a look' alarm stays.

Fix: (1) Home is long. Fold the setup band into track-graft's one-line strip ('1-2-3 · Next: choose your own password →') so To do and Lately added rise above the fold. (2) Balance the plates' names by words, not length, so 'Mount St. / Helens day trip' does not break inside a proper name. Keep: the box first and widest on the left, the starters' 'usually X' hints, the 'Continue with Vera' terminus, the departure board listing all plans, the compact setup notice and To do's Now split. Fix: (1) The enamel starter faces are close in value. Make the hint's destination word match its page icon (calendar, checklist, bulb) so it reads without colour. (2) Give the To do ring-tick a visible affordance: a hover and focus fill, a check that previews on hover, and an aria-label 'Mark done'. Keep amber for the 'late' margin words, not the ring you press. (3) On the phone, stack the starters instead of scrolling them sideways behind a fade. Fix: (1) Make the tube shorter (drop the weeks strip on Home or fold it into the tube's footer) so Coming up rises above the fold. Keep the board fed by the lit wire at NEXT UP and the slim top setup bar. Fix: make To do's date windows plain inset readouts with no button-like border, and keep amber for the words only. Put the kids' wishes on the rail as a stop, or in the right column, so visual and Tab order agree. Bring the sub-44px Home target up to size.

Keep the one-line setup and To do beside the box. Fix: drop the bordered who-tags for a plain ink name with a person glyph, so they stop looking like buttons. Set the pencil 'how far off' in the voice face italic rather than Victor Mono, cutting the faces to three.

If the instrument panel is kept, give the spend meter a scale that shows a usual day mid-arc (a log or day-limit scale), and put the six-signal key wherever the signals appear (Settings, To do), or cut them to three easily told shapes.

a.titles: Best: 'What's our plan?' (t3-track-refine, t3-timetable-refine, t3-timetable-mut, t3-pocket-refine). It is short, in the family's own voice, invites them to tell Vera something, fits one line on the phone, and lights the job word. 'What's the plan?' (t3-track-refine2) is a near-equal, more casual and kitchen-table, and it reads well over the starters branch. 'Tell Vera our plans.' (t3-timetable-graft) is the clearest for a newcomer, because it names who hears you. But it is an instruction, not an invitation, and the full stop needs special handling. 'What needs planning?' (t3-track-graft) is a good invitation that cannot be answered no, but the long lit word is heavy. 'What should we plan?' (t3-pocket-graft) is fine but sounds unsure. Weaker ones: 'Anything to plan?' (t3-pocket-mut) invites 'no', and 'What are we planning?' (t3-track-mut) reads as a status check.

a.notes: Typographically the heat splits in two. Pocket Diary, Kept and Departures, Hung each have a type system a typesetter would sign off: dates set one way everywhere, numbers tabular and in columns, markers hung outside the text edge, a heading face with a clear job. The track series has the best plates (Trued, Relit) but no settled date convention: '9 Oct Fri', 'Sun 27 Sep 19:56' and 'Sun 27 Sep' with 'was due' under it all appear in the same lineage. Grafts that worked: hung kind labels in Lately added (Ticked); dotted leaders (Hung, Printed, Platformed, and the boards); column heads on To do (Relit). Grafts that did not work: the Victor Mono cursive pencil (right idea, wrong face); the amber date pills (Printed), which are cramped; the separate full-stop span. Every lineage shows invented '19:56' due times, which are noise and should go. The phosphor returns typographically best when it lights a few words (the key word, the board, Vera's newest line) rather than haloing body text.

scores.why: DM Sans and DM Mono with a flat hierarchy. To do shows ISO dates ('Due 2026-09-27 19:56') in cards, the title is barely larger than the section heads, and the figures don't line up in columns.
Plex Sans and Plex Mono form a tidy desk-terminal system. Times and costs are tabular in right-hand columns. But the mono labels are small and tracked, and the head scale is shallow.

The diary dates are set well: a large figure with the month and day stacked beside it, times in a tabular mono column, and Instrument Sans heads. The tracked LATER/SOMEDAY plates and the footer key are noise.
The wide Archivo title at 2.75rem has presence, and the departure board's leaders are good. The body type and labels sit too close in size, and the counts are set loosely.
Archivo condensed heads over DM Sans give a clear title. The plates' readouts (09:00 in a mono well) are good, but the To do date column and the small plate text crowd together.

Same faces as its parent, set more carefully. A full-width condensed title, plates with name, mono time and relative time on one baseline, and a tidy right-aligned date column on To do. About 100px of empty glass breaks the rhythm under the starters.

Best typesetting in its lineage. Plate titles at a real heading size, kind labels over them, times in sunk mono wells, numbered setup steps, and a To do table with Due/Who/When heads. Minus: the noisy '19:56' times, 'Mount St. / Helens' broken inside a name, and a mixed date stack ('4 Oct Sun').

The largest, boldest headline in the heat, 'What needs planning?', reads first and well. Lately added hangs its kind words in a right-aligned margin column, a good typesetter's move. On To do, each date carries a second amber 'was due' line, which crowds the margin.
The parent's type is unchanged. The new meter and lamp labels are tiny tracked mono capitals, which is a step back in legibility on Status.

Clear one-column reading order. The dotted leaders in Lately added and the wishes are a nice touch. The Archivo title is heavy beside light body text, 'usually Plans' is set in a weak grey, and there are many sizes with no clear steps.

The departure board's leader dots and the banded rows read like printed timetable paper. The condensed amber date pills on To do are cramped. The title's full stop sits in its own span and gives an odd space. Archivo body and heads are unchanged.

The only real new type system in the heat: Barlow Condensed for signs and figures, Red Hat Text for the voice, and every marker and number hung outside one text edge. On To do, hung '#4' numbers with leader dots run to the late words. Bold condensed amber at 13px is heavy, and the footer quote hangs past the right margin.

The most consistent typesetting. Every date is set the diary's way (a big tabular figure with month and day stacked in mono), times sit in their own column, condensed Instrument Sans heads hang from one spine, the measure is sensible, the setup steps are numbered in boxes, and To do lines up in a clean table. Small faults: the tracked mono 'Someday' plate, and names that no longer line up.

Victor Mono italic as 'pencil' for how far off a thing is ('in 7 days', 'was due 5 days ago') is a real typographic idea with a job. But its cursive 'y' and 'g' sit awkwardly beside Plex, four faces is too many, and the ink who-tags weigh more than the titles they label.

Keeps Pocket Diary's good date setting. The halo on Vera's chat words and on the lit times brings the tube back in the right voice, but the glow softens body text at 16px, and the prompt cursor in the box reads as typed text.

The base typesetting is sound: a condensed head over a clean grotesk body, mono kept for times, dates in the day stacks and the month's figures, and drive times in the Ideas table set right-aligned and tabular. Against t3-track-refine2, though, Coming up's plate names are set small and in body weight, the counts are stacked in tiny type ('4 coming / next...') that breaks the heading's baseline, and To do's 'N days ago' in mono sits awkwardly against the sans rows. That makes it a modest step up from today's, about level with t2-track-graft.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the date setting (big tabular figure, stacked month and day, separate time column) as the app-wide date standard, and the spine with condensed Instrument Sans heads. Fix: set the Later/Someday/Now plates in sentence case without tracking (or Instrument Sans 600) so they match the heads. On To do, put the 'who' back in its own fixed column, about 120px, so names line up. Drop the meaningless '19:56' times when a due date has no real time. On Home, the 'Each one is a short page' note in the setup list needs a step more space above it.

Keep the Barlow Condensed signs / Red Hat Text voice pairing and the hung markers on one text edge: this is the strongest type system in the heat. Fix: set the amber late words in Red Hat Text 500, not condensed bold, because the condensed face at 13-15px looks weak and too heavy at once. Raise condensed labels to 600 at 15px or more. Keep the footer quote's hang inside the page margin. Ship Barlow as two weights only (500, 600) to cut the 18 files. Give Home's middle column 26px back so long titles don't wrap. Bring the denim spine back to the family's chat plates.

Keep the plates with a kind label, a heading-size title, and the time in a sunk mono well; the numbered setup stops; the To do table with Due/Who/When heads. Fix: break plate titles with balance but no-break inside proper names (nbsp in 'St. Helens'). Set the date stack as figure then 'Oct' over 'Sun', both in DM Mono at one size, as on To do. Drop the clock times on To do unless they were set. Tighten the gap between the 'Coming up' count and the Google note to one leading step.

Keep the full-width box title and the one-baseline plates (name / 09:00 / in 7 days). Fix: close the empty glass under the starters by pulling Coming up up to the tube's top. Put To do's 'was due…' under the title instead of in the date margin, so the margin carries only the dates.

Keep the big headline over the box and the hung kind words in Lately added's margin. Fix: To do's two-line amber margin (date plus 'was due') is too dense: keep the date alone in the margin and put 'was due' after the title in ink-2. The setup strip's 'All 3 steps' link is set smaller than its row, so match the sizes.

The pencil idea is worth keeping, but in a calmer italic: use Plex Mono italic or Instrument Sans italic in graphite rather than Victor Mono's cursive. Cut the faces to three. Make the who-tags plain text with a person glyph, so the titles carry more weight than their tags.
Keep the halo on Vera's words, but weaker: a 0 0 6px glow at about 25% for body text, so 16px text stays crisp. Keep the lit times. Drop the false caret before the placeholder.
Keep the board's leaders and the banded rows. Widen the amber date pills, or set them without a box as amber tabular text. Join the full stop to the title, or drop it.

a.titles: Best: "What's our plan?" (t3-track-refine, t3-timetable-refine, t3-timetable-mut, t3-pocket-refine). It is short, in the family's own 'our', sits on one line at display size, and lights one 4-letter word that is the job, so the halo stays compact. Second: "What's the plan?" (t3-track-refine2). It sets as well, but is a touch less the family's own. "What needs planning?" (t3-track-graft) invites well, but the 8-letter lit word is heavy at that size and the line is long on a phone. "Tell Vera our plans." (t3-timetable-graft) names Vera and the job, but the imperative with a full stop reads like an instruction, and the stray period hurts the setting. "What should we plan?" (t3-pocket-graft) is fine but a little hesitant. "Anything to plan?" (t3-pocket-mut) can be answered 'no'. "What are we planning?" (t3-track-mut) reads as asking how things stand, not as an invitation to tell Vera something.

a.notes: Grafts that worked for usability: the one-line setup with its next step named (timetable-graft, pocket-graft), which frees space for To do near the box; To do beside the box (pocket-graft); and destination hints on the starters (timetable-refine). Grafts that did not: the stop as the tick on track-graft (its hidden affordance, and the same shape means 'status' elsewhere); the boxed ink who-tags (they look clickable); the cursive pencil face (hard to read); amber-outlined date windows (they look like buttons); and the dimmed late words. No design here has small targets (all 0 under 44px except timetable-graft's 1) or overflow. Text minimums are 12-13px, but the pocket designs drop to 11.5px on the phone. Recurring phone fault: the sideways-scrolling starters (track-refine, track-graft, pocket-refine and pocket-graft) hide two of three ways to start. Stacking them, as track-refine2 and the timetable designs do, is better. Line-heavy month grids (track-refine2's rail per week) cost the 'find a date' task. A rail is best only where there is an order (To do, setup, chat).

scores.why: Every task is findable, but text bottoms out at 11.5px, 42 targets on Home are under 44px, the green glare tires eyes at night, and To do's cards with 'Edit, complete, or snooze' folds make ticking off a slow two-step job.
Calm, consistent and every target is 44px or more; the tracked capitals and the dense side panel still make Home slower to scan than the best of this heat.

Clear lamps and a readable To do, but on desktop the question sits right of the tube, so the eye lands on NEXT UP before the box. Plan plates are small, and the Plans month rail is extra ink for the job of finding a date.
The box comes first and setup has a 'Next step'; Coming up spends a lot of height on a rail with small plates, and the phone shows only the top of Coming up before the fold.

The full-width box under 'What's our plan?' is now clearly where you start, the setup steps say 'Next step', and To do has real checkboxes with dates. About 100px of empty glass separates the starters from Coming up, the plates are small, and on the phone the ways to start scroll sideways and hide two of them.

The most self-explaining Home in the heat: 'Or start with' rows with arrows, plates big enough to read with kind, who and a time well, setup with a lit Next step, To do with checkboxes, full dates and late words, and the kids' wishes at the foot. On the phone the starters stack. Costs: the Plans month runs a rail through every week row, which is clutter when you only want a date, and Coming up pushes To do below the fold on a laptop.

The compact setup strip and 'Next: choose your own password' are quick to act on. But on To do the ring on the rail IS the tick, and a first-timer reads an amber ring as a status lamp, not a button (it is a button for screen readers, but nothing on sight says 'press'). The setup strip hides what each step is for, and the phone starters scroll sideways.

The parent's usable Home, unchanged. The new Status meter crowds the zero end and reads as empty at a glance, its 14px signals are hard to tell apart (dashed socket against ring), and the legend lives only on Status.
Box and starters first, a clear setup card with 'See all', compact lists; its steel line and denim plates were quieter, and its kind rings carry no words on Home.

Very easy to start: a big 'What's our plan?' over the box, three stacked starters that each say where they lead ('usually To do'), a lit 'Continue with Vera', explicit checkboxes with who and late words, and '9 parts · 1 needs a look' heading Settings. Weaknesses: the NEXT UP board's dot-matrix rows are small mono text to read at night, and on Settings and the Status rows each value sits at the far right, a long sight line from its label.

Setup shrinks to one line with 'Choose your own password' and '2 more', which puts To do near the top. Its date windows ('Sun 27 Sep') are amber-outlined boxes that look like buttons, the late words were dimmed to grey so 'late' rests on the ring alone, and the kids' wishes sit off the line in an odd Tab position.

One clean text edge helps scanning lists, but condensed Barlow labels at 15-16px read light, Chat's family and Vera bubbles are now told apart mainly by side, and the hang narrows Home's middle column for typing.
Legible diary rows, real checkboxes, Now and Later make order obvious; the setup card is long and pushes things down, and the footer key repeats on every page.

Calm and plain to use: the box first, numbered setup steps you can click, a To do column with checkboxes and late words, and diary dates easy to read. The phone box is tall, so Next starts at the fold. On Plans the glowing mini month is small for picking a date, and the starters still scroll sideways on a phone.

To do beside the box and setup as one 'Next: Choose your own password' line are real wins for getting things done. But the ink who-tags are boxed like buttons and invite useless clicks, the late notes in Victor Mono cursive italic are the hardest text on Home to read for tired eyes, and four faces is a lot to learn.

Lighting Vera's words and the one key to press does help find Send and tell the speakers apart in Chat. The lit cursor bar in the empty box looks like text already typed, and the green readout columns on Ideas compete with the content.

fixes.suggestion: Keep: the 'Or start with' branch of arrowed rows, the plates with kind, who and a sunk time well, the setup row with a lit Next step, and To do's full date and time column. Fix: on Plans, take the rail out of every week row of the month and keep only the current week's now run, so finding a date is a grid again. Plate titles should break at a word boundary, not inside 'Mount St. / Helens'. Let To do sit beside Coming up on wide screens (or fold setup to one line once step 1 is done) so the overdue items show without scrolling. Give the phone's 'who is asking?' select room for its chevron.

Keep: the stacked starters with 'usually Plans / To do / Ideas', the lit 'Continue with Vera' terminus, the explicit checkboxes and the 'N parts · 1 needs a look' summary heads. Fix: set the departure board's rows at about 15px proportional, or in VT323 at 1.2rem, so they read at night. On Settings and Status, pull each value next to its label (a fixed 14rem label column) rather than flush right. Put the Kind field's chosen state visibly apart from its placeholder (a real select, or an ink value).

Keep: the one-line setup bar ('Finish setting up: Choose your own password · 2 more') and To do raised beside the box. Fix: make the date windows flat text with an amber ring dot, not outlined boxes that look clickable, and bring back the amber late words beside them. Put the kids' wishes on the right under Lately added, so the Tab order matches what you see.

Keep the structure as it is. Fix: on the phone, shorten the box (a two-line placeholder, From and Send on one row) so Next shows above the fold, and stack the three starters instead of scrolling them sideways. On Plans, make the mini month's days 32px or larger, or make the agenda's day headers the jump targets. Explain the filled steel node in Status's key.

Keep To do beside the box and the one-line setup stop. Fix: unbox the who-tags (an icon and plain ink text, no fill or edge) so they stop reading as buttons. Set the 'how far off' notes in the body face in italic, not Victor Mono cursive, so they can be read at a glance. Drop to three faces.

The idea of a lamp that is also a switch is good, but it needs an affordance: draw an empty checkbox-sized ring (24px or more) with a faint tick on hover and focus, put a 'Tick when done' hint in the column head, and keep the amber late colour for the words rather than the ring that is pressed. Restore each setup step's 'so the family can…' clause under its ring on hover or at desktop width. On desktop, put the question above Vera's tube so the box is read first.
If the meter stays, use a log or 'usual day' scaled dial so a $0.04 day reads, and put the six-signal key on Settings and To do too, or drop the dashed socket in favour of words.

a.titles: The best is "What's our plan?" (t3-track-refine, t3-timetable-refine, t3-timetable-mut, t3-pocket-refine). It is short, fits one line on any phone, invites you to tell Vera something, says the job in one word, and 'our' is the family's voice. A close second is "What's the plan?" (t3-track-refine2): just as clear and short, a little less warm. "What should we plan?" (t3-pocket-graft) works and is explicit, though slightly longer. "Tell Vera our plans." (t3-timetable-graft) is the clearest about who hears you and what the box does, and it is good for a first-time user. But as an imperative with a full stop, it reads less like a box's label, and the separately spanned period is read with a gap by extractors. "What needs planning?" (t3-track-graft) is fine in meaning, but its 8-letter lit word is heavy and it reads like a to-do audit. "What are we planning?" (t3-track-mut) reads as a status check. "Anything to plan?" (t3-pocket-mut) invites a yes or no rather than a message. All are better than "What's on your mind?", which never says what the box is for.

a.notes:
Skeptic's summary:
- Nearly every design still risks the subway map. Rails appear on Home, To do, Chat, Status and Settings in all three lineages, so the lines must earn their place by marking an order (time, steps).
- Amber is still over-used as box outlines and chips in t3-track-refine, t3-track-graft and t3-timetable-graft, which makes the pages read as warnings.
- The navy/ink plates in the track series are the main costume risk: solid blue slabs beside green.
- Grafts that worked: the lit wire feeding the departure board (timetable-graft), To do's tick-as-stop (track-graft), the compressed setup line (pocket-graft), the steel starter branch (track-refine2).
- Grafts that failed: Victor Mono pencil cursive (pocket-graft), amber date chips (timetable-graft), quotes on the starters (timetable-mut).
- Two mutants carry ideas worth keeping that their lineages should absorb, though by themselves they change too little of the page (the owner's 'nearly identical' test): track-mut's instrument Status and pocket-mut's glow on the machine's voice.
- Yardsticks: today's page is still the Matrix. Desk Terminal is coherent but tool-like. The heat's best now match or beat it on structure and fall short only in finish.

scores.why: Still the Matrix: green everything, ~83% green share, flat cards, the greeting is a corner box. Has the original glow, and nothing else.
Coherent and calm, but the mono-heavy desk terminal leans toward an editor theme. The tracked caps and tiny labels make it read like a tool more than a family page.
The lit sill line has soul, but the now lamp spills past the board's edge. The amber-boxed setup panel reads as a warning, and the tube and question compete side by side.
The tube hangs below a rail with a big empty slab of glass beside it, and the starters float in an empty right column. A lot of line for little order.

The full-width question box is right. But the now lamp's lit run stabs out of the board's left edge, there is ~100px of dead glass right of the tube under the starters, and the whole setup card is outlined in amber, which reads as an alarm.

The cleanest track design: the steel branch of starters off the box is the best use of the line language, the setup steps read as a route, and the lit word glows. But the navy plates are big solid slabs that drift toward 'navy UI kit', the lit run is a stub, and the tube is crammed into the plate row.

The one-strip setup and the To do ticks as stops are real gains, and the headline is big and lit. Faults: the board splits into tube-left / question-right, so the question is not first; amber setup rings read as warnings; right-aligned kind labels sit oddly left of the icons in Lately added.

Status is the best in the heat: a named lamp board and a moving-coil meter in real phosphor. But Home, Chat, Ideas and Plans are pixel-identical to the parent, so it fails the owner's 'nearly identical' test everywhere but one page.
The three columns squeeze the box into a narrow middle. Green share near 89% is back toward the Matrix, and the board out-glows the question.

A strong reorder: Vera's line on the left with a large lit question, the departure board beside it, quiet dotted leaders. The skeptic's knocks: the enamel keys are fragile and the plum one reads muddy-purple, the amber left bar on setup is warning-ish, and the grounded colour is mostly hairlines.

Feeding the board on a lit wire from the rail is the heat's best single graft, and the banded rows and departure list read as one station. But three amber-outlined date chips on To do shout alarm at the top right, and the long lit vertical rail is close to glare.

The condensed sign face gives real typographic character. But quote marks round the starters look as if they get sent, the box column is cramped between two side columns, and Chat goes 97% green: the Matrix again.
The time spine is a genuine structure, but the parent still carries tracked caps and the amber '6 worth a look' alarm.

Now/Next/Later on one spine is the clearest page structure in the heat. The Coming up rows with big day figures are a typesetting win, and amber is confined to late. Weak points: the tracked Now/Next/Later pills still feel costume-mono, and the setup list in the right column is heavy for a one-time thing.
Pencilled Victor Mono cursive italic for 'in 7 days' and 'was due yesterday' is a costume, and the navy who-tag chips clutter every row. The compressed setup line and To do beside the box are good.

It answers the owner's 'bring the glow back' best: Vera's chat lines are lit screens and the family's stay matte, a real rule. Elsewhere it is the parent unchanged, and it keeps the amber alarm on Status.

Fix: tone the navy plates down to slate with only the cyan cap, so solid navy stops dominating Coming up. Give the tube room: let it stand as stop one's plate at the same height as the others, or move it beside the box. Lengthen the lit run from now to the tube so the motif reads. Keep the full-width question box. Stop the now lamp's run at the board's inner edge, not outside the card. Fill or close the dead glass right of the tube by putting the starters under the box. Swap the amber card outline on Finish setting up for a slate card with one amber ring at the step that needs doing.

Keep Vera's line on the left, the big lit question and the board beside it. Replace the plum enamel key with a calmer slate-plum, or drop the tinted faces and keep only the coloured stub.
